blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Existing referring segmentation methods on Gaussian scenes primarily target whole objects, relying on segmenter-generated candidates from which a vision-language model (VLM) selects. Such predetermined fixed candidates may omit fine-grained parts needed as targets or cues for identifying objects. We introduce SplatScout, a query-driven, closed-loop approach that places perception under VLM control. The model actively selects views, directs segmentation, and inspects rendered 3D results to refine its predictions. For part-level evaluation, we introduce PartRef-ScanNet++, comprising 261 manually verified queries across 12 ScanNet++ scenes with mesh-derived ground truth. On PartRef-ScanNet++, SplatScout achieves 0.538 mIoU, substantially outperforming existing methods. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of iterative refinement, while comparisons across VLM backbones highlight the importance of effective tool-feedback utilization. SplatScout also achieves higher scores on four existing referring benchmarks. Code and the PartRef-ScanNet++ benchmark are available at https://github.com/kaust-violab/SplatScout.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
3D Gaussian Splatting ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) represents scenes as explicit
primitives that can be reconstructed and rendered
in real time. Beyond rendering, a growing body of work attaches
language to Gaussian scenes. Open-vocabulary methods distil features
from 2D foundation models into Gaussian primitives, enabling
category-level queries ( Qin et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) .
Referring methods go further, identifying specific objects described
by expressions involving attributes and spatial
relations ( He et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2026c ; Ding et al., 2026b ; Hassan et al., 2026 ) .
However, existing referring methods for Gaussian scenes primarily
focus on whole objects, while practical instructions often refer
to their parts, such as “the handle of the second drawer on the
right of the table by the window”. Unlike whole objects, parts
have query-dependent granularity: the same chair may be requested
as a whole in one query, its backrest in another, and its armrest
in a third. Parts may also serve as targets, discriminators
between similar objects, or anchors for locating other objects.

Grounding such expressions requires identifying
the relevant scene regions and segmenting them
at the granularity specified by the query.
Suitable observations must be selected to obtain
segmentation masks across multiple views, which
are then integrated to construct the target
Gaussian instance. However, the required views
and segmentation regions depend on the query
and may only become apparent during perception.
A fixed, query-independent scene decomposition
therefore cannot reliably provide all the
candidates needed for grounding.

blocks.en:
Meanwhile, modern vision-language models (VLMs)
are increasingly capable of recognizing visual
attributes, distinguishing fine-grained regions,
and reasoning about spatial relationships in 2D images.
Yet many existing grounding methods limit the VLM
to selecting candidates proposed by a segmenter,
either during preprocessing or in a single pass
at query time. Even when candidates are generated
on demand, the VLM typically cannot use intermediate
visual feedback to revise them. Consequently,
if the target part is missing or segmented at
the wrong granularity, stronger visual reasoning
alone cannot recover it through candidate selection.
This design limits how effectively advances
in VLM capabilities translate into better grounding.

blocks.en:
We address this limitation by changing the role
of the VLM from candidate selection to perception
control. Rather than choosing from a predetermined
set of instances, the model decides where to look,
what to segment, and at what granularity,
based on the expression and its observations.
The segmenter and geometric operations become
tools that execute these decisions, allowing
the VLM to apply its visual understanding
directly to the construction of query-specific
3D instances.

However, query-time perception alone is insufficient
if decisions are executed in a single pass.
The appropriate next action often depends on
previous results: an observation may require
closer inspection, segmentation may reveal
an incorrectly selected region, and lifting
the masks into 3D may expose errors that
were not apparent in the original images.
We therefore organize perception as a closed
loop in which each operation returns feedback
to the VLM. By inspecting intermediate results,
the model can revise its decisions and progressively
refine the target rather than committing
to its initial predictions.

blocks.en:
On this basis, we introduce SplatScout, a query-driven,
closed-loop perception system for referring segmentation
in Gaussian scenes. Before a query arrives, SplatScout
never constructs semantic candidates.
During query execution, the VLM coordinates
three tools: the Navigator selects informative
observations, the Segmenter produces query-directed
masks, and the Lifter constructs 3D Gaussian
instances. Each tool returns feedback that
informs subsequent decisions, including rendered
views of lifted instances for detecting
and correcting errors. The VLM thus controls
both instance construction and the decision
of when to return an answer.

To evaluate part-level grounding, we introduce PartRef-ScanNet++,
a benchmark containing 261 manually verified referring
expressions across 12 ScanNet++ ( Yeshwanth et al., 2023 ) scenes. It covers whole
objects, parts serving different roles in referring
expressions, and multiple-target queries, with ground
truth verified on laser-scanned meshes.
On this benchmark, SplatScout substantially
outperforms prior referring segmentation methods
and achieves higher scores on four of five existing
referring benchmarks. Controlled experiments
further investigate the benefits of closed-loop
perception and the role of VLM capabilities
in utilizing perceptual feedback.

visual feedback to guide perception, particularly for

expressions across 12 ScanNet++ scenes and an evaluation

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Gaussian Splatting ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) represents
scenes as explicit primitives that can be
reconstructed and rendered in real time.
Many works attach language to these primitives,
primarily enabling open-vocabulary segmentation
through object names or category labels rather
than full referring expressions.
They train features from 2D foundation models
into per-scene fields ( Qin et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) ,
attach semantic information to Gaussian
groups ( Ye et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Xie et al., 2026 ) ,
or back-project features without
training ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Marrie et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2026a ; Chacko et al., 2025 ; Zang et al., 2026 ) .
ReferSplat ( He et al., 2025 ) extends language-based
Gaussian segmentation to full referring
expressions by training a referring field
per scene. These approaches rely largely on
pre-established semantic representations,
rather than constructing target instances
through query-driven perceptual interaction.

blocks.en: A second line brings in a vision-language model at query time, but these methods restrict its use to choosing among candidates that a segmenter has produced. On Gaussian scenes the candidates are instance groups or a scene graph built once per scene ( Hassan et al., 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026b ) , or masks cut once at query time from a class label parsed out of the expression ( Ding et al., 2026c ) . On point clouds they are a lookup table of segmented objects that the model reasons over before selecting an ID ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . OpenGround ( Huang et al., 2026 ) and Think, Act, Build ( Wang et al., 2026 ) segment a missing label on demand, but only to extend the existing candidate set in a single query, and without any check in 3D. Similar to VLM-free methods, all of the above only select among pre-segmented candidates, without enabling the VLM to use its perception to explore the 3D scene or guide the segmentation with expressions based on scene and query understanding. In this work we focus on adding this capability to the VLM.

blocks.en:
Existing part-aware Gaussian methods such as
LangSplat and its successors ( Qin et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Chacko et al., 2025 ) primarily rely on SAM and CLIP models to create pre-generated whole-object,
part, and sub-part masks and language embeddings. Their supported
granularity is therefore limited by the
regions identified during preprocessing.
On point clouds, part-level understanding
has been studied mainly through functional
elements. SceneFun3D ( Delitzas et al., 2024 ) annotates handles, knobs, and buttons
referenced by task instructions.
Subsequent methods ground such parts using
2D detectors and segmenters ( Corsetti et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) or fixed superpoints ( Wu et al., 2025 ) .
Anywhere3D ( Wang et al., 2025a ) evaluates
bounding-box grounding across granularities,
while Articulate3D and MultiScan ( Halacheva et al., 2025 ; Mao et al., 2022 ) provide detailed part annotations.
Existing benchmarks primarily treat parts
as predefined targets, with limited coverage
of their roles in identifying other objects.
In contrast, PartRef-ScanNet++ includes parts as
targets, discriminators, and relational
anchors, with mesh-level segmentation
ground truth. SplatScout supports these
different roles through query-adaptive
part segmentation.

blocks.en: 3.2 Method Overview

blocks.en:
As illustrated in Fig. 1 , SplatScout
consists of three functional tool sets coordinated by a VLM
controller: the Navigator, Segmenter, and Lifter. Starting
from the desired output, obtaining the target Gaussian subset
requires constructing 3D instances from multi-view segmentation
masks, which in turn requires acquiring suitable observations
of the scene. These dependencies define the responsibilities
of the three tool sets. The Navigator retrieves informative
scene views, the Segmenter produces query-directed masks,
and the Lifter integrates multi-view masks into 3D Gaussian
instances. Their complete interfaces, including available
actions, arguments, and feedback, are listed in
Table 5 of Appendix A .

We introduce PartRef-ScanNet++, a benchmark for part-level
referring segmentation comprising 261 manually verified
queries across 12 ScanNet++ scenes. The queries reference

objects, parts as targets, parts as discriminators,
parts as anchors, and multiple targets. In 154 queries
(59%), parts serve as targets, discriminators, or
anchors. Each query was manually reviewed to ensure
unambiguous target identification and
natural, contextually appropriate wording.

with existing benchmarks are detailed in

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We introduced SplatScout, a query-driven,
closed-loop approach to part-level referring
segmentation in Gaussian scenes. By placing
perception under VLM control, our method
enables the model to select observations,
construct query-specific instances, and
refine its predictions through perceptual
feedback without precomputed semantic candidates.
We also introduced PartRef-ScanNet++, a benchmark
covering diverse part-level referring expressions
with mesh-derived ground truth.
SplatScout substantially outperforms existing
methods on our benchmark and achieves higher
scores on four external referring benchmarks.
Our experiments further demonstrate the
benefits of iterative interaction and show
that feedback from different perceptual
stages plays complementary roles.
These findings highlight the potential
of closed-loop perception for leveraging
increasingly capable VLMs in fine-grained
3D scene understanding.
